stories.title: Why Checking on Grandpa Really Matters
stories.headline_kid: Experts in Singapore say older men need more care and company, because big life changes like retiring can make them feel very lonely.
summary: When people grow old, many things in their lives change. They stop working when they retire, their children grow up and move out, and sometimes their husband or wife passes away. All these changes can leave older people spending a lot of time alone.

A Singapore helpline called Samaritans of Singapore (SOS) shared sad news: last year, most seniors who died by suicide were men. Doctors say this happens because older men often face many hard changes all at once — losing their job, their health, and their friends — which can pile up and make them feel very low.

Experts also think many older men were taught when they were young to 'be tough' and not talk about their feelings. This means they may keep their sadness bottled up inside instead of asking for help, which can make things worse over time.

The good news is that small actions can help a lot. Visiting grandparents, calling them for a chat, or simply asking 'how are you feeling today?' can remind them that they are loved. If someone seems very sad for a long time, it's important to gently encourage them to talk to a counsellor or call a helpline.

lenses.me: You can make an older person's day brighter just by chatting with them or asking about their hobbies.
lenses.family: Spending time with grandparents — even a short phone call — can help them feel less alone.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates could start a small habit of greeting elderly neighbours or helpers at school.
lenses.nation: Singapore has a fast-growing number of elderly citizens, so caring for them is becoming more important every year.
lenses.world: Many countries with ageing populations, like Japan and South Korea, face the same challenge of keeping older people connected and supported.

stories.title: New Faces Join Singapore's Top Team of Leaders
stories.headline_kid: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has quickly brought several experienced government workers straight into his Cabinet, the team that runs Singapore.
summary: Singapore's Cabinet is like the country's leadership committee. It is a group of top ministers, led by the Prime Minister, who make big decisions about things like schools, hospitals, jobs and housing.

Recently, PM Lawrence Wong picked a few people who used to work as senior civil servants — that means they used to help run government departments behind the scenes — and made them Ministers much faster than is usually done.

A newspaper commentator explained that PM Wong did this because he currently has fewer fresh choices for new political leaders. Bringing in experienced public servants gives Singapore steady, capable leadership, even though it means the Cabinet may not have as many different kinds of backgrounds as before.

Having ministers from different walks of life — business, unions, grassroots work — helps the government understand more types of problems that ordinary people face. This is why many people hope future Cabinets will include even more variety.

lenses.me: The people in Cabinet decide things that affect your school syllabus, your family's cost of living, and even your future job opportunities.
lenses.family: Ministers make policies about housing, healthcare and CPF that shape your family's everyday life.
lenses.friends: You could discuss with classmates what kind of leader you think makes the best decisions for a country.
lenses.nation: A strong and steady Cabinet helps Singapore plan carefully for the future, even during uncertain times.
lenses.world: Other countries watch how Singapore chooses its leaders as an example of stable, long-term governance.

stories.title: Japan Earthquake: Factories Stop as Death Toll Rises to 35
stories.headline_kid: After a huge earthquake in Japan, 35 people have sadly died, and factories that make cars and computer chips have had to stop working.
summary: Three days ago, a powerful earthquake struck the Kumamoto area in Japan, causing a shopping mall to explode and collapse. Rescuers, helped by sniffer dogs, finished searching the rubble on Friday. Sadly, the death toll has now reached 35.

The earthquake also badly damaged factories that make cars and computer chips — the tiny electronic parts found inside phones, laptops, and even cars. Many of these factories have had to pause their work because their buildings were damaged or they lost electricity.

This matters beyond Japan because factories there supply parts used all around the world, including in gadgets we use in Singapore. If factories stay closed for long, it could mean fewer new phones or cars being made, and prices for electronics might rise later on.

On top of this, tens of thousands of people in the affected area still have no electricity or water, and temperatures are expected to reach almost 40°C this weekend — making it even harder for people to recover and rebuild their homes.

lenses.me: The phone or gadget you use might contain a computer chip made in Japan, so this earthquake could affect how soon new gadgets are made.
lenses.family: Your family might notice slower deliveries or higher prices for electronics and cars in the coming months.
lenses.friends: It's a good chance to talk with friends about how disasters far away can still touch our daily lives through trade.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports many electronic parts, so this reminds us why it's wise to have backup suppliers from different countries.
lenses.world: It shows how connected the world's factories are — a disaster in one country can affect products used everywhere.

stories.title: Malaysia's Neighbouring State Votes for New Leaders
stories.headline_kid: Today, people in Negeri Sembilan, a Malaysian state close to Singapore, are voting to choose who leads their state government.
summary: Just like Singapore has different towns, Malaysia is divided into states, each with its own state government. Today, on 1 August, voters in Negeri Sembilan are casting their votes to decide who will run their state for the next few years.

This election is an important test for Malaysia's Prime Minister, Anwar Ibrahim, and his coalition called Pakatan Harapan. His group did not do well in a similar election in Johor — another state near Singapore — a few weeks ago, so people are watching closely to see if he can win back support.

Rival political parties are trying to attract voters by focusing on shared Malay and Muslim identity, hoping this message will unite enough people to beat Anwar's coalition. Both sides have also been promising young voters better jobs, homes, and improved public transport.

Malaysia is Singapore's closest neighbour, connected by the Causeway that thousands of people cross every day for work or school. A stable government there matters to Singapore too, because it affects trade, food supplies, and the ease of travelling between the two countries.

lenses.family: Malaysia supplies Singapore with some food, like vegetables and eggs, so its politics can sometimes affect prices at the market.
lenses.friends: Friends whose families have relatives in Malaysia might talk about this election at home.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies on good relations with Malaysia for trade, water, and daily travel across the Causeway.
lenses.world: This election shows how democracy works — citizens voting to choose who represents and leads them.

stories.title: Shanti Pereira Races Into the Commonwealth Games Final!
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's fastest woman, Shanti Pereira, ran in the 200m final at the Commonwealth Games and finished eighth against the world's best sprinters.
summary: The Commonwealth Games is a huge multi-sport event where athletes from many countries — including Singapore — compete against each other, much like a giant sports carnival held every four years.

Shanti Pereira, Singapore's top sprinter, made it all the way to the final of the women's 200m race. She finished with a time of 23.21 seconds, placing eighth among a very strong group of runners from around the world.

Even though she did not win a medal this time, reaching the final of such a big competition is already a huge achievement. It shows just how much hard work, discipline and talent Shanti has put in to represent Singapore on the world stage.

Shanti has already made history for Singapore in athletics before, and her performance continues to inspire young Singaporeans to take up sports and chase their own dreams, whether they end up winning a medal or not.

lenses.family: Your family can cheer for Team Singapore together and talk about the value of trying your best, medal or not.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could chat about which Commonwealth Games event you enjoyed watching the most.
lenses.nation: Shanti's efforts show Singapore's growing strength in track and field on the world stage.
lenses.world: Her performance reminds everyone that small nations like Singapore can still compete bravely against sporting giants.
